speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, I would like to propound a question or two to the government and also to make a complaint-shall I say?-regarding answers to questions, particularly to one question to which I am now going to refer. I am not objecting to the right of the government to refuse an answer provided they take the responsibility of so doing, but answers when given should be accurate and complete,

Japanese Immigration
because we depend upon the information given lby the government for our guidance in considering public affairs.
I wish to draw the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to an important question that I put on the order paper the other day and that was answered yesterday, a question regarding immigration. The third question was as follows:
Has the government entered into a new agreement covering Japanese immigration with the Japanese government? If so, has a quota of 150 been fixed upon?
The answer to that was:
As a consequence of negotiations between representatives of the governments of Japan and Canada last year, the Japanese government undertook to restrict to 150 annually the number of Japanese emigrants going to Canada as household servants and agricultural labourers.
The next question was:
If a quota has been fixed, does the said quota include all classes of immigrants, such as merchants, students, etc., or are such admitted in excess of the said quota?
The answer to that was:
Answered by the answer to No. 3 above.
The inference being that the total restriction was to 150. In the agreement between the government of Canada and the government of Japan, a copy of which I have in my hand, provision is made for four or five classes of immigrants. For instance, there is the class which includes those previously resident in Canada, and the wives and children of such. Then, there are those who are in domestic service, when evidence of engagement is given. Then there is this class,-and this is of vital importance: provision is made for the admission of contract emigrants. These are hot covered in the answer to my question, and the result is that the whole situation is left in a vague and ambiguous state. In addition to that, there are emigrants brought in under contract by Japanese resident agricultural holders. Now, these are not necessarily included in the answer given, which refers to agricultural labourers and domestic servants. So, the answer does not, in reply to my question, give that light and information to which we think we are entitled. That is my complaint. I wish to ask the Prime Minister if he would have this previous set of questions again surveyed and a more complete answer given.
Secondly, I want to ask him in connection with this very vital and important matter whether he has noticed a despatch from Tokio stating that in view of the dispute between the American government and the Japanese government, the latter consider themselves
freed or liberated from all obligations to restrict emigration from Japan to Canada or Mexico, citing as the ground for their repudiation of these agreements the fact that when the gentleman's agreement was entered into with the United States some years ago Japan agreed with the United States that they would enter into similar agreements with Mexico and Canada as an additional protection to the United States. There was the suggestion in that connection that the so-called underground route was being frequently used and that immigrants were smflggled in from both borders. Now', the Japanese government declare that since the United States has passed legislation which they declare objectionable they are at liberty to repudiate both the agreements referred to, namely, that with the Mexican government and that with the government of Canada. If the Prime Minister has not noticed this I would draw his attention to it and ask him to make careful and early inquiry in order to provide for the protection of Canada in case the Japanese government actually give effect to this statement issued from Tokio yesterday.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I gave the
House the information the other day, in reply to a question by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) or some hon. member on that side of the House. There is a very serious controversy between the city of Chicago and the surrounding states which are opposed to the diversion of the water at Chicago. Canada has never admitted that it agreed to the diversion of a foot of water through the Chicago drainage canal. True, the Secretary of War for the United States gave permission to the Chicago drainage district to divert 4,167 cubic feet per second. Since that time it is estimated that they have increased that diversion to 10,000 cubic feet per second, which is estimated to be the amount passing through at the moment for the purpose of diluting their sewage, and hence the controversy is going on between the United States and all the states and cities surrounding Chicago within the area of two or three hundred miles. It has been a matter of litigation in the courts. We have been watching that litigation very carefully. The government of Canada have repeatedly protested officially to the British Embassy against further diversion of this water, or against any diversion, maintaining that we have not agreed and do not propose to agree to any diversion of water through the Chicago drainage canal. The solicitors who are appearing for the Chicago drainage system state that in a memorandum prepared by the old waterways commission, prior to the inception of the International Joint Commission, when the question of diversion for power purposes at Niagara Falls was under discussion, there was a reference to the Chicago drainage scheme. Hon. members know without going into detail that there is at the present moment a considerable portion of that power passing every year into the United States for the use of the factories of that country, something in the neighbourhood of 160.000 horse power is being exported. But that did not at any time form any part, so far as I or any of the officers of the department can discover of the reports submitted to the government of Canada, nor was it ever admitted by the Dominion of Canada. That is the position the government is maintaining still. To say that we should get into a controversy when the matter is at present in the courts, or was up to a day or two ago, and is being vigorously protested against by all the people surrounding that district and all the
Supply-Interior

people affected by it, particularly the city of Milwaukee and all the cities along the shores of lake Michigan would hardly seem to me to be proper. I do not think at the present time we should do more than we have done in this matter.
A committee of the United States senate are investigating this matter, and will present a report to the senate with respect to the whole controversy, and the best information we can get is that there is not a very serious likelihood of Chicago being able to maintain its position, but Canada has from time to time registered her protest in the proper channel and we have been kept fully informed of every move in connection with this controversy.

I would like to call to the attention of the minister the claim made on behalf of the Chicago Drainage Commission in connection with the arguments at Washington regarding this water diversion. It was suggested that Canadians were taking more water from lake Erie for electrical power purposes than they were entitled to take under the treaty arrangements between the two countries, and the fact was instanced that the Cataract Power Company, which is developing electrical power at Decew Falls and taking water for the purpose of electrical development at the Welland canal, was drawing from lake Erie water in excess of what Canada was entitled to take under the treaty arrangements. I think it will be well for the minister to emphasize the fact that the Cataract Power Company is not taking one gallon of water from lake Erie beyond what would be taken for the purposes of navigation of the Welland canal. The Cataract Power Company is taking simply surplus water, water which would not be used for the purposes of navigation even if they did not take it. There is a large volume of water in lake Erie from the summit level of the Welland canal to the brow of the mountain which is about fourteen miles from lake Erie where the locks begin. The Cataract Power Company is taking simply the surplus water which is not required beyond that fourteen mile limit for the purposes of navigation of the canal. The same quantity of water would be flowing through the canal even though the Cataract Power Company was not using the water at all. Therefore, the argument of those who maintain that Chicago is entitled, based on that suggestion, to 10,000 cubic feet per second, is absolutely erroneous and the minister should emphasize that, so far as he can, in the discussions that are taking place.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The importance of the
Chicago drainage canal diversion is sinking home pretty deeply into the minds of the Canadian people. It has been impressed upon us with greater and greater emphasis for years. It is costing us more, month by month, and year by year. The utter callousness of the whole proceeding on the part of the Chicago drainage canal district is becoming more and more brazen, and surely we must now realize that any pressure of mere words, particularly of mere letter writing, is not going to get us anywhere in rescuing us from the position we are in. The Chicago drainage canal district is extracting 10,000 cubic feet per second from our waters, or rather from the joint waters of the two countries. It is lowering the level of our lakes and of our rivers. It is destroying the efficiency of our' canals. It is costing in our shipping millions per annum. It is costing in the upkeep of our canals millions more. This is being extracted out of the pockets of the tax-payers of Canada and is being paid for by the sweat of the people of Canada. I do not think I overstate the case when I say that it is all utterly without any colour of right whatever. To argue that behind the pages of the treaty which gave us a right of power development and them a right of power development at Niagara, and beneath the lines of that treaty, there was a reason for the larger percentage of the power being given to us in the fact that Chicago had a certain water diversion, seems to me so sophistical, so grotesque, that I cannot understand how it appeals to those who dignify it with the name of argument. The treaty speaks for itself. By the terms of the treaty, by every line and letter of it, we are ready to abide; but we do not like to be referred to what is supposed to have been in the back of the head of somebody who wrote it, and it does not seem to become the dignity of a great country to ask us to be so referred.

It is getting to be of vital consequence to the Dominion, and I press upon the government the need of exerting more pressure than mere pen and ink. Something must foe done.
I do not use that language in
9 p.m. any threatening sense; but I do say that there are powers of pressure in our hands, and we ought to gather all the strength behind our motion that we can put behind it in order to get this thing to a head quickly. We should not depend upon the mere rights of litigants as between the city of Chicago on the one hand and the United States government on the other. Our controversy is not with the city of Chicago. Our controversy, necessarily, is with the government of the United States. We look to the government of the United States to stand up and see that justice is done as between that country and our own.
I do not know that we are in a very dignified position when we appear as being represented the same as an American town or a county or a village before some committee of the United States senate. A committee of the United States senate is not the tribunal before which we should go. We go to the United States government and we say to the United States government:	There is our
right; that right you admit; that right no sensible or fair-minded person can dispute; that right we call upon you to make good. I know that all matters of international negotiation are very difficult, but I think it is well that in this parliament we should stand up and speak our minds. We have submitted to this thing year after year, and from one decade to another and thus submitting, the iron has -been pressed into us deeper and deeper. The prospect of relief seems to me to be getting less and less. The penalty is getting heavier and heavier. It is when we find ourselves in situations of this kind that we realize how we need the united effort of us all and the influence that we all can exert together-when I refer to "all", I mean the Empire as a whole-in order to bring to us our rights in this regard. I know of nothing more vital to Canada than that we should now get to the point where there is going to be an end of this continuous and increasing diversion at Chicago.
The minister is quite right. We have never agreed to the diversion of a foot of water; we have tolerated it year after year, and our toleration has been played upon and imposed
upon by the Chicago drainage canal district, multiplying its diversion time after time until now they have it at a stage where at least the volume stated by the minister, if not a great deal more is being wantonly extracted. They actually contemplate -going further and further. I have stated my position, and I am ready to support the government in bringing to bear the utmost pressure in its power upon the United States government, and in so directing its policy that it will be able to gather other forces at its side for this purpose.

Can the position be properly taken by Canada that the United States is liable for all damages which our people are suffering by reason of this diversion? It seems to me that if the United States is allowing one of its states to break the treaty governing the control of these waters, and in consequence we are suffering millions of dollars damages, the government should make a claim for those damages as well as a request for the cessation of the illegal diversion.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the hon. members who have just spoken have tried to impress on the government the importance of this matter. I should like to speak of it from the western viewpoint. It has been proven beyond doubt that the level of the waters of the upper lakes has fallen two or three feet in the last year or two. I do not know just how much water is taken out by the Erie canal, nor how much is used for power purposes on the Niagara river. I was wondering if the minister had collected any data to indicate exactly to what extent the water level in the upper lakes has been lowered by the Chicago drainage canal diversion. At the investigation which took place in Washington a short time ago I think those who represented Chicago let the cat out of the bag by indicating that they had some hope of making the canal a transportation channel to the Mississippi river. I do not know to what extent they are using it for transportation purposes now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, for transportation
and power.

It is not necessary now, I think, to repeat what has been stated several times in this House, that the western provinces find it very difficult to compete in the markets of the world, and that the saving of a few cents per bushel on the transportation of their grain means a great deal to them. I remember reading some time ago in a departmental report issued by the United States government that after a large vessel
Supply-Interior

is loaded down to about fifteen or sixteen feet the loss of one foot in the water level means a loss of 980 tons of cargo-carrying power. I have made some calculations which lead me to believe that that estimate is about correct. One can readily see what it means to have the level of the upper lakes lowered about 24 feet and the large freighters forced to make their trips with only part of their full cargo. It means extra charges, and, as we know, all the charges are thrown back on the producer. In other words, if we are compelled to pay 3 or 4 cents per bushel more for the carriage of our grain to Montreal, we will receive that much less at the country elevator. If that is continued, and perhaps made worse, so that our loss becomes heavier in future years, it will mean that Russia, the Argentine and other wheat producing countries will have a still greater advantage over us than they have at the present time in the grain markets of the world. In a report by Secretary Wallace of the United States Department of Agriculture I notice that in making some comparisons he stated that the Argentine has an advantage over Canada and the United States in transportation of about 10 or 12 cents a bushel from the fact that very little grain is grown in the Argentine at a greater distance than 400 miles from tidewater, and most of it is grown much nearer, and that while the grain growers have to pay a higher rail rate, yet it is only for a very short distance, and this gives them a considerable advantage. So the minister can readily see that everything should be done in order to cheapen our transportation rates. I am very glad that the discussion has taken place, and I hope that the minister will realize that written protests should now give place to something stronger, if this is possible.

Mr. Chairman, I wish
to associate myself most emphatically with every word that has been uttered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in regard to this matter. Those of us who live on the water transportation routes appreciate the fact that the lowering of the water level by a few inches means, not thousands, but millions of dollars extra in the cost of transportation; and we know that the water levels of all the Great Lakes are being lowered by reason of this diversion.

And all down
to the sea.

Yes, I believe it affects
the St. Lawrence as well. The city of Toronto in their corporate capacity sent representatives to attend the meetings in Wash-IMr. Millar.]
ington. I strongly urge on the government the advisability of engaging someone who is thoroughly conversant with all the circumstances and to send him to Washington to protest authoritatively on behalf of the Canadian government against the Chicago drainage canal diversion. So far as I know there has been no real protest on behalf of the Canadian government. I thoroughly agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition that an effective protest should be made, not by municipal representatives, but officially by the government of Canada to the government of the United States against the violation of the treaty, coupled with a request that the violation should be stopped by the United States government preventing the, city of Chicago continuing this illegal diversion. I would strongly urge on the minister the importance of the government taking prompt action to put a stop to this violation of our treaty rights.

I should like to associate myself with this protest. There is an aspect of the question which I have not heard touched upon, that of expense, which is of the utmost importance to the Dominion. At the present time there is a pronounced drop in the level of lake Superior, whether due to the Chicago drainage canal diversion or not I do not know, for it is argued by some authorities that the upper lakes are not affected by the operation of that canal because of the natural outflow of the upper lakes into the lower.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think
they mean lake Huron and Georgian bay.

At any rate there is a
very marked drop in the level of lake Superior; I forget the exact amount, but I think it is about a couple of feet. Whether or not it has any bearing on this question I do not know, but if you lower the lake levels it means that millions of dollars have to be spent on the hafibours in order that the boats may enter them as they have done in the past. The harbours at the head of the lakes, for example, which are built not for the benefit of the head of the lakes alone, but for the whole of western Canada, have had something like thirteen or fourteen millions spent on them in dredging, the construction of breakwaters, and so on. The same is very largely true of the harbour at Toronto and of all the harbours on the Great Lakes- Goderich, Owen Sound, Kingston, Prescott, Port Colborne, and others. If the water level is lowered to any considerable extent it

Supply-Interior
means the expenditure of additional millions in order to deepen the harbours sufficiently to permit* the continuance of navigation. I do not think any of us can add strength to the protest offered by the right hon. leader of the opposition, with which apparently everybody in the House agrees. I sincerely hope the government will do everything in their power to impress on the government of the United States the importance of this question to Canada.

Perhaps the minister
might give the committee some information as to what protests have been made on behalf of the government of Canada, with details as to when they were made and what was the character of them, together with any communications received in reply. If the government has not taken any action by way of protest they have been derelict in their duty. The situation is apparently becoming very acute. Besides, Canada should be placing herself in a position where it cannot be said by the United States that we have stood by and allowed this diversion to take place without protest. If it is true that the treaty which has been referred to provides against any such diversion as we are complaining of, then necessarily there will be a claim on behalf of Canada for damages or compensation. Now, we should be laying a foundation for that claim; we should be pointing out to the government of the United States that we intend to make such a claim. Certainly we should not sit down and take all this kind of thing without doing anything. If the government can say that everything possible has been done, very good, but we surely ought to know about it. There is no occasion for secrecy in a matter of this kind; on the contrary, it is one upon which I think the committee and the country are entitled to be fully informed.

It is hard to estimate the importance of this question, to the people of Canada. I would like to associate myself with what has been said by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in respect to this diversion of water. It very seriously affects all the lower lake levels. I have the honour to represent a portion of the country which may be very vitally affected if this diversion continues or is in any way increased. Millions upon millions of dollars have been spent not only in the harbours and along the lakes and rivers but also in dredging the channel in the river St. Lawrence. This channel has had to be repeatedly dredged and deepened, and if the
water level is to be lowered by continued diversion it will simply mean that constant deepening and dredging of the river channel will be necessary. The question is important also from the point of view of power as well. Water diverted at Chicago might otherwise be available for the development of power at Niagara and be used over and over again on the river St. Lawrence. So that the damage that has already been done to Canada and that may in the future be done if this diversion is not stopped cannot be overestimated. I would support the government in their doing something more than entering mild protests at Washington against the diversion of this water at Chicago. I think the time for mild protests has long since passed; something a little bit more effective might be done in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What would my hon. friend suggest?

Yes, I know, and the hon. member sat down, perhaps rightly thinking that the government, which is charged with the responsibility of preserving Canadian rights, will do something to preserve them. I will ask my hon. friend this question: Why is it, as the government sees it, that specific Canadian rights not only are flaunted and disregarded but continue to be flaunted and disregarded? What reason can the government give the committee?

Apparently everybody in the House admits-not only admits, but claims-that diversion is going on and going on, that lake levels are dropping and dropping. Mr, STEWART (Argenteuil): No one recognizes better than my hon. friend does that there are international courtesies with respect to all these matters. I feel just as strongly as the right hon. leader of the opposition does about this matter. I feel that Canada is entitled to redress, as the hon. member for Centre Toronto, I think, suggested-more than that. Any one who is following this controversy must know that Chicago has been offering foi a considerable period of time to make redress for the diversion. Do you think it would be wise for the people of Canada to offer to take any redress for the diversion of 10,000 feet of water which belong to the Great Lakes and to the waterways of Canada? That water should be returned to the Great Lakes, should not be diverted at all. Rather than have payment for diversion we should have the water returned to us. That is the position this government takes.
Well what are you doing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
What are
we doing? We are courteously, as any government would do, as the government of my hon. friend would have done, protesting against this diversion of water, and saying that we do not agree to a single inch of it going, and never have agreed. At the moment, as I have pointed out, we are working in conjunction with the solicitors who are protesting in the committee and in the courts against this diversion. Are not all the American cities situated along the Great Lakes- Buffalo, Detroit and so on-affected as well as Canada? Undoubtedly they must be. But I am not putting that up as a reason why we should let up one iota in our protests with respect to this matter.

Are not the American
municipalities also protesting?
Mr, STEWART (Argenteuil):	They are
fighting it to the last ditch, every one of them, and we have working with those gentlemen an engineer who knows more about this waterway, I think, than any other man in Canada, in the person of Mr. W. J. Stewart, who has more information on this subject, so far as I have been able to ascertain, than any other man that I know of. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that the present government have not been recreant to their trust. My hon. friend points out that the water in the Great Lakes is going down. I do not admit that; I say that the present height of water is largely attributable to the diversion at Chicago. That is the position of the Canadian government and we are endeavouring to have that 
water restored to its natural channel. That is also the position that is taken by the solicitors who are fighting this case on behalf of all the interests surrounding the great city of Chicago. The Chicago people are putting up the best fight they can at every step in this controversy. This government is watching the case, and we have protested, and protested most vigorously, against this diversion of water, but beyond the point of courtesy we have not gone.
In answer to my hon. friend from New Westminster we have tabled copies of the correspondence passing between the twq governments. I most heartily concur in the view that our course should not be to protest before a committee of the senate or in the American courts, but to the American government itself. So, Mr. Chairman, I do not admit that this government has been recreant to its trust. So far as I am able to advise the government, I would advise the most strenuous action to be taken if it should appear that this thing was to continue.

How much
longer will it be necessary for it to run before it is apparent that it is going to continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far as I am aware, there has not been any further diversion during the last two years, but 10,000 cubic feet have been going for the last two years at least through that canal.

My hon, friend, of course, has an intimate knowledge of the subject which I have not. All I see is what the press says from time to time. But according to some articles I have seen in the press, apparently the city of Chicago is under the impression that it can increase the flow of water through the existing canal just as it pleases, and is doing it. That may be all wrong, but that is the impression, nevertheless, and we have to1 an increasing degree lowness of water. My hon. friend is quite light when he says we should get our water back. There is no dispute about that. But what are we doing to get it back? That is what we are trying to find out. My hon. friend says Canada's case is not for a committee or an American court. Canada's case stands on international rights and should be adjudicated according to international rights. Am I right in supposing -that every protest that could be taken by the government in connection with the preservation and enforcement of Canada's rights has been taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That might be a matter of opinion, but as my hon. friend well knows, Canada has never taken any other

Supply-Interior
position than that, either through this government or the former government. We do not admit their right to divert a single foot of water. As I said, Chicago has made tentative suggestions, not to the Canadian but to the United States government, to substitute dams to increase the height of water, but those works have never been recognized by the Canadian government, and I think should not be recognized by us, as a substitute for the water itself. What we want is the water. We do not want any substitution works to compensate for the diversion of that water. That is our position, and that is the position we propose to maintain.
Have you raised this question directly with the American government?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have not raised the question. I doubt whether this is the proper moment, and whether we are not in a better position, at least, this is the advice I have to offer, to maintain our rights by demanding the return of the whole of that water, than to begin to negotiate about the matter. I think this government would be well advised, before agreeing to any reference of any character, to be very sure where it is going to lead them. We are standing firmly on the ground of demanding the return of that water. Undoubtedly this question could be a matter for reference to the International Joint Commission.
What does the minister mean by the return of the water?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Shutting off the Chicago diversion entirely. We cannot expect that to be done all in a moment, but that is the position for us to take.

You cannot get water
returned that has been taken down to the gulf of Mexico. The point, as I see it, is whether this government should do something more than simply fail to concur. The government, it seems to me, should go further than that. It should take active steps to protest directly to the American government against what is being done; otherwise, it may be held that this government has acquiesced.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Oh, no, I
thought I had made that very clear.
In answer to a question that was asked by the hon. member for South York the minister, as I understood him, said that the government had not taken any active steps at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Will this
satisfy my hon. friend? The position of this government has been outlined repeatedly, and our position is that we have not agreed to the diversion of a single foot of water. We have objected to the diversion strenuously. Some hon. gentlemen have said that it has been a sort of passive objection. It has not been of that character at all. All these suggestions that I have mentioned have come from the city of Chicago. The city is fighting American municipalities along the lakes, who are objecting just as strenuously as we are, and who, I take it, are being affected as adversely as our Canadian municipalities along the Great Lakes.

To whom have our
objections been made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
made objections through the British Embassy, to the American government. Copies of them are on file here, and my hon. friend can read them all. I want to make it clear that we have not at any time agreed to the diversion of a single foot of that water, but on the . other hand we have protested against it strongly. Of course, I do not expect to get back the water that has gone down to the gulf, but I do hope to put a barrier across the mouth of that canal and stop any more water going down.
Have the protests been made directly to the government of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Will the minister tell us what answers the government of the United States have made to those protests?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The answers are all in the record.

The discussion on both sides of the House has been very unanimous. One would have thought that the municipalities along the lower Mississippi, in view of the great difficulties on the lower Mississippi river and the enormous cost of building dykes to prevent flooding great areas, would have been adverse to Chicago diverting a large amount of water from the Great Lakes. This is a very serious matter. The greatest inland waterway in the world seems to be in peril. The diversion of water affects lake Ontario, lake Erie, the St. Clair river, lake Huron, lake Superior and lake Michigan as well as the cities located on the shores of these great lakes. A number of American cities are alive to the danger involved as well as
Supply-Interior

ourselves-notably Buffalo, Cincinnati, Detroit Superior and other cities. These great communities are acting jointly in an effort to prevent this diversion by the Chicago sewerage system.
Then there arises the question of what shall be done in the case of power developed on the St. Lawrence and the Great Lakes system. One of the worst features of the proposed joint hydraulic development on the St. Lawrence is the exportation of power to the United States. It is contended by some people in this country that if power is allowed to be exported to the United States that in the course of three or four decades a sort of vested interest will be established and any move to discontinue that exportation even in the interest of Canada herself will be met with strenuous opposition. Accordingly it is argued that Canada cannot consent to any such exportation because in the course of time it will be instrumental in building up towns and cities in the United States, whose industrial life would depend upon its continuance and they would fight to the utmost [DOT]to prevent a termination of the contract. That is one reason why I am emphatically opposed to the exportation of power developed from Canadian sources to the United States.
I am glad to see to-night such a unanimity of opinion on the question of the diversion of water for the Chicago drainage canal. It is well that the message should go out to Washington that the representatives of the Canadian people in parliament assembled are determined to safeguard, as far as they can, the maintenance of the level of the Great Lakes, and that they are desirous of preserving for Canada her share of the waterpower capable of being developed on the St. Lawrence. I am glad to add my voice to what appears to be the unanimous opinion of hon. gentlemen, regardless of party, on this question.

I wish to say to the minister that it appears to me from his statement that he is considering the situation from the point of view that certain states of the United States are to-day litigating with the city of Chicago to prevent what is going on. Now,
I wish to point out that our rights are not dependent on any legal proceedings between different states of the union and the city of Chicago; they are treaty rights which are not in any way connected with such litigation. That being the case we have no particular reason as a country to wait until the states m question litigate with the city of Chicago; we have no interest in such a matter as that

at all. Our duty as a country is to see that our treaty rights are maintained and that they should not be interfered with in a manner that is obviously causing damage to the people of this country from a power point of view and from the point of view of what is happening to Canadian harbours. That is the real matter at issue, not the awaiting of the result of litigation between certain American states and the city referred to. It seems to me, with all respect, that the government's right, under the treaty, is one that should be enforced in the strictest possible fashion, dealing directly with the United States government. Let the other parties to whom allusion has been made fight the matter out among themselves.

I should like to ask the minister whether he has had any consultations in regard to this question with the joint committee which has been appointed to consider the question of the St. Lawrence waterways and the canals?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The International committee has been called together for June 11, when this matter may be discussed by them. I am very much pleased that this discussion has taken place because, I think it is well for the United States to know how the Canadian parliament feels on the subject. I think that rather than resenting the raising of the question the minister will welcome this discussion. I am sure it will be pleasing to the people to know that the House of Commons of this country is standing up firmly for Canadian rights. The matter is one that concerns the governments of the two countries. I agree thoroughly with the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol)' that although there may be litigation awaiting decision, although a committee at Washington may be considering the question, our rights in this matter stand on much higher ground. The government of Canada, on behalf of the Canadian people, claim that Chicago has no right to continue the diversion of water, part of which belongs to the Dominion, without our consent. Now, our consent to that diversion has not been and will not be given. Such action as we are taking is being taken through the government as a whole and not by any particular minister. I can confidently assure the House that the government is taking every step which the situation calls for, not through any sort of side-door action, not keeping in mind any particular litigation; we are not going to pre-suppose that our rights stand on that

Supply-Interior
kind of basis. We are going to stand on the treaty rights which Canada possesses, and we propose to do everything possible to see that those rights are maintained.

I thoroughly agree with the remarks made by previous speakers on the subject of the diversion of water from the 'Great Lakes by the Chicago Drainage Commission. However, that is not what I rose to speak about at the present time. I wish to call the attention of the minister to a matter which I have already drawn to his notice this session. I think the matter has also been brought to the attention of the government on various other occasions. It is the question of the diversion of water from the St. John river to the Penobscot river by a dam at a place called Chamberlin lake on the Allagash river. The dam and the stream are in the United States, but the stream itself is tributary to the St. John river which is international boundary water for a short distance and then becomes Canadian.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
Are the dam and the
stream in the United States?

Yes. There is Chamberlin lake on the headwaters of the Allagash river, and the natural outlet of this river is into the St. John which is a Canadian river. There has been a dam built which prevents the flow of the water out of the natural channel. An artificial canal has been constructed to divert the water into the Penobscot river. This was done some years ago, and I believe no protest was made at the time. It was done by lumbermen, not under any international agreement whatever, but done by lumbermen who wanted to drive logs down the Penobscot river, in order to get an additional supply of water. However, at the present time the government of New Brunswick is making a survey of St. John river at a point near Grand Falls for the purpose of developing water power, and this diversion of water will be a very serious handicap to this enterprise. I called the attention of the minister to this matter some weeks ago. I do not know whether he has made any inquiry, if he has not I wish he would. I understand that some time after this dam had been built a protest was made . by the Canadian authorities, but there was a tentative agreement entered into when the protest was made by Canada that the dam would be allowed to stand as a wooden dam, not of a very permanent character, but that they would not be allowed to rebuild it; and that when the immediate necessity to drive lumber was over, 175

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: the dam should not be rebuilt, and the water should be allowed to return to its natural channel in due course. That time has arrived and we want that water now possibly worse than we ever did before or ever will again. It will be impossible to make improvements in the development of the water power at Grand Falls if this dam remains. The hon. member for Restigouche and Madawaska (Mr. Michaud) knows very much more about this than I do. He represented Victoria county previous to the year 1917. I think he took the matter up on previous occasions, and I would like him to give the minister the benefit of his views.

In 1842 a treaty was negotiated between the United States and Canada in connection with the American boundary between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine. This treaty is called the Ashburton treaty, and it was understood between the two countries at the time *the treaty was signed that, in order to develop industries, to encourage trade and commerce and to facilitate transportation between the two countries, the St. John river should be made an international boundary, and when we speak about the St. John river it includes its tributaries. The Chamberlin lake is at the head of the Allagash river. In order to divert the water from the Allagash river the lumbermen of the state of Maine went to the legislature at Augusta and obtained authority to dig a canal from the Chamberlin lake into the Penobscot river. In doing this they diverted the water from the Chamberlin lake, and prevented it running into the Allagash river, so that the whole of the water of that lake ran into the Penobscot river. The people of New Brunswick objected to the company being authorized by the state of Maine to dig a canal in order to divert that water. At first the state of Maine refused to allow this company to go to work, but about twenty or thirty years ago the same company obtained authority from the state of Maine, and began to dig their canal, and diverted that water. Since that time our province has protested against such diversion of water. During the first or second year I was in the House of Commons I brought this matter up, and it was understood that it would be taken up with the authorities of the state of Maine. A few years afterwards-I think about the year 1909 

the International joint waterways commission was appointed by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Mr. Barnhill was on that commission, I think.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Supply-Interior

Yes, and I believe the commission is still in existence. We Canadians have been endeavouring to persuade our American friends to remove that dam at the foot of Chamberlin lake, and to give us an opportunity to have all this water which should come to us. One of the great disadvantages caused by the diversion of this water is that in the spring of the year, or in the latter part of June especially, we are driving into the St. John river from the headquarters about 500 million feet of lumber. When the water runs down very rapidly all that lumber floating down may go to the shore and ground there. On one or two occasions we had to go to the state of Maine and beg them to close up the dams, and let the water from the Chamberlin lake run into the Allagash river and the St. John river. I say that they have monopolized entirely the waters of that river; and, judging from what my hon. friend has said, this is not confined to districts where I live, or the district where the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) lives, but it applies to all the waters for a distance of about two hundred miles. The St. John river is navigable from St. John to Fredericton, and we feel that we suffer a great loss by the diversion of this water, because it interferes with the transportation of lumber and affects our trade and commerce as far as Fredericton. I hope the Minister of the Interior will take the matter up. I think the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton brought this question up in the early part of the session. We are very much in earnest, and we feel we have been more or less abused by our American friends. If we let them go ahead in the future I do not know what will become of the country.

I think the House is entitled to more information on this question. It was debated one afternoon some time ago, and at the request of the government it was laid over to be brought up again. I am not satisfied that the minister and the department are doing all that could be done in this matter. At the present time in many of the harbours on our Great Lakes, such as lake Erie, lake Ontario and in many ports on the St. Lawrence, the depth of water is from two to three feet lower than it was some years ago. The question involved is the construction of the boundary waterways treaty of 1909 made between Great Britain and the United States. There is no reference to Chicago in that treaty, and the word "Chicago" is not even mentioned in it from beginning to end. It is true the Chicago people had the consent of one party to the treaty-the United States-to

taking 4,167 cubic feet per second, but they have not the consent of the people of Canada or the people of Great Britain to the diversion of even that much water. The matter is now before the courts, the judges found against the diversion, and now an appeal has been taken to the Supreme Court of the United States, but in the meantime the damage done to Canadian interests amounts to $35,000,000 a year. That is the commercial value of the power which could be developed from the water which is being pilfered by the Chicago drainage people. Deputations from Canada are now going down to Washington, and it is rather humiliating to the people of this country to find that over the head of the British government, over the head of the Canadian government and over the head of the British Embassy at Washington, private deputations, who do not represent the people of Canada are appearing before the Rivers and Harbours committee of a foreign country. It is not in keeping with British institutions and traditions that deputations should be appointed and should appear before a committee of the congress of a foreign country on this particular question. It is all very well to make a protest. For 15 or 20 years protests have been made in regard to this matter. Every port on the Great Lakes is in jeopardy in this matter. The diversion is interfering with the interests of trade and commerce and the power interests of Ontario and Quebec are in jeopardy to-day as a result of the diversion.
Millions of dollars are being wasted every year. The time has come for something more vigorous than mere protests or sending some minor official of the minister to Washington to look after a matter like this. The time for protests has gone by; the time has come for action. What is the International Joint Commission for? Is it just to be a debating society? The boundary waterways treaty was discussed in this House in 1909 for days and weeks. Is it to be turned into a scrap of paper by the government of the United States? We are told that Canada is a nation. If Canada is a nation, let Canada be up and doing and put a stop to this pilfering and theft of water, contrary to the waterways treaty, by the government of the United States. It is all very well to talk, but the government of the United States is responsible for this Chicago diversion of water in excess of what is allowed by the treaty. It will be very serious for the public works at different ports along the rivers and lakes of this country if this question is to be made a political football. While the

Supply-Interior
Canadian government is not a party to the treaty, the government of Great Britain is a party and the government of the United States is a party. Not one word of the treaty mentions the Chicago drainage system at all. That came in as an afterthought. They are not authorized by the treaty to take any water.
Before the Rivers and Harbours committee in the United States they are criticising the government of Ontario for taking water from the	Chippawa canal. The
Ontario government are taking 12,000 cubic feet less than the treaty gives them. The treaty gives them about 32,000 cubic feet; they are exporting 12,000 cubic feet of that to the United States, and the United States which are allowed 24,000 cubic feet, have in addition 12,000 cubic feet of Canada's allotment of 32,000	cubic feet, so that the
United States are getting 36,000 cubic feet and Canada is getting only about 20,000 cubic feet. Therefore, that argument before the Rivers and Harbours committee is an utter fallacy. They have not a leg to stand on before the courts. Judge Landis rendered a decision granting an injunction against them and they went to the Supreme Court, of the United States. They are at present before the Supreme Court of the United States and the bill before congress is just a bill to kill time.
If we are a nation, let us, by all lawful means, put a stop to this thing, have it abandoned, and let the party responsible for it be brought to time by the government of Canada. If we are to believe what the government say about Canada being a nation, if Canada is a nation, let us see that our treaty, the treaty of Great Britain, which is to-day being turned into a scrap of paper by the people of Chicago, is respected. The Chicago authorities are preparing plans now for a diversion of 20,000 cubic feet a second, and they are seeking to have a canal going away down through the United States, following the Ohio and Mississippi rivers right down to the gulf of Mexico. That is where the water of the Great Lakes will wind up. What is the use of protesting to people like these? They do not respect the treaty; they do not intend to respect it; they have treated it as a scrap of paper. On the government of the day is the responsibility, because the provincial governments, the municipalities, the harbour boards of the country, the Dominion Marine Association, the navigation interests, right up to the head of the lakes, have all protested, but their protests might just as well not have been made. The time for talk has 175J
gone by and the time for action has come. The minister has not been as alert as he might have been in connection with this particular question. We want our treaty carried out to the letter. Instead of merely protesting, we should see to it that a treaty entered into solemnly by the United States government and the British government is lived up to The government of' the United States would not tolerate for one moment the city of Hamilton or Windsor or some other Canadian city attempting to divert fifteen, twenty or twenty-five thousand cubic feet of water from the Great Lakes. Canada has kept her part of the treaty to the letter. She has given the United States of her allotment 12,000 cubic feet of water for the development of electrical power in that country.
I do not say that the present minister is altogether responsible for the present situation, because he has been in the department for only a couple of years. Still, there should be some negotiation between the two governments. The International Joint Commission is empowered by the waterways treaty to make an investigation. What has become of this commission? Are the commissioners receiving their salaries now and are they able to take care of this question? Coming from a large city, greatly interested in this particular problem, and coming from the province of Ontario which is interested from a navigation and light and power standpoint, I wish again to register my protest against the way in which this matter is being dealt with by all concerned. It is the duty of the people of the United States to bring the Chicago drainage canal district to time. We are part of the British government. Let us conduct our protest through the British government, the Canadian government and the British Ambassador at Washington and not have a large number of deputations going to Washington and making protests. The protests should go through the proper channel and not through provincial and municipal channels.

I should
like to present the case from another point of view. Ontario is largely interested with the United States on the borders of the St. Lawrence river in the development of horsepower, and there is a great demand for that horse-power now. As Sir Adam Beck pointed out not long ago, in certain eastern Ontario towns there is a growing scarcity of power. That power is limited by the quantity of water, and if the water is diverted at Chicago, there will be less power at Cornwall island. Ontario has a real interest in that power and does not want to be deprived of a single
Supply-Interior

horse-power of it, but wishes to get her full share. Ontario is as much interested in this matter as other portions of the country, and the government ought to move rather rapidly in securing our rights in this matter.

I rather agree
with some of the last statements made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church), that if this treaty is negotiated between Great Britain and the United States, the proper course for the govern-10 pm. mcnt would be to seek the assistance of Great Britain to see that the treaty is lived up to. But I think the hon. member for North Toronto used rather strong language when he suggested that we should repudiate a treaty that had been entered into solemnly between the two countries. Surely there is a better way of dealing with the matter. Surely some negotiations can be entered into whereby this matter can be adjusted without sacrificing the honour of the Canadian people and possibly the honour of the British Empire. I think we are using fairly strong language when we go that far.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Prince has entirely misunderstood the tenor of the remarks which were made by the hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Church). He does not seek to have anything repudiated; all he desires is that sacred international obligations should be lived up to, and that the government should see to it that nothing is left undone to ensure their observance. I agree with a great deal of what has been said by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). It is a good thing that everybody ehould know where we all stand in connection with this matter. Canadian interests are really very much greater and very much more important than we have yet had pointed out to us, because the farthest western part of the prairies is to-day interested in the navigability of the water route to the St. Lawrence, and to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec the maintenance of the water level is absolutely vital. For example, what is to happen to the large interests in Ontario of the Hydro Electric Commission, and the large interests in Quebec of the power companies if their waters, which are international waters, can be withdrawn without reason and without excuse, contrary to all the provisions of international treaties made between civilized nations in this century? It is a very important question for them. Now, in view of the assurance given by the government I am going to take it for granted that they realize the seriousness of this matter.

At an earlier part of the discussion I asked for particulars of what protests had been lodged by the government with the United States government, and my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said that a return had been brought down. I have not had an opportunity of seeing that return. I have no doubt it was my fault, but I frankly say I did not notice that the return had been tabled. Unless my hon. friend says something to the contrary, I am going to take it for granted that that return will give all the information which the government thinks ought to be disclosed at the present time.
