Some time ago I pointed out to this House that in considering the sources of revenue from the natural resources of this country, the tourist traffic should rank third. I agree with the minister that probably enough money has been spent in the western parks of Canada. There are a great many other sections of this Dominion immensely suitable for the attraction of tourist traffic; and I feel that if some method were devised whereby we could co-ordinate the various tourist associations of this country under one head, say the Parks branch, and concentrate our efforts upon the development of the tourist traffic, it would be a good thing for Canada.
Has the minister under his hand a list of the historic sites which are marked this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would it meet the request of the hon. member if we would prepare a list and either give it to Hansard or send it to him? It is sometimes difficult to segregate them here. We will be glad to file a list.
If the information is not right at hand I would not press it.
Was the question with regard to the sites to be marked this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I brought to the attention of the department last year a site in the province of New Brunswick which I think should be marked. It is the site of the old fort at Meductic, on the St. John river. The landmarks are becoming pretty well obliterated, but it would be possible at the present time to locate this old fort. It was an important point in the early history of the province of New Brunswick I think, if I am not mistaken, that some officials in the department told me it was up for consideration last year. Has it been considered this year, or a little more than considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The superintendent tells me that it will be under consideration by the board to-morrow.
Is the electric lighting plant that the minister referred to completed and in operation, and if so, what is the total cost of that plant to the department?

I notice a part of this item is to reimburse the provincial government for salaries of police magistrates at Banff and Jasper. Will the minister explain that item.
Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have
been having some difficulty in connection with the administration of law and order in the park. We have, as you know, the Mounted Police looking after the park; we have many tourists there and frequently have rather difficult cases to be taken care of in a magisterial way. Formerly, under the act, the magistrate at Banff was appointed by this government. We have now asked the provincial governments to appoint the magistrates and we pay them.
How much under this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $2,600 to the magistrate at Banff and $2,200 to the magistrate at Jasper.

The parks are not
within any municipality?
No.
I presume the magistrates are required for the purpose of enforcing the regulations in the park?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For all purposes, yes.
I suppose the cases which come before the magistrates are mainly breaches of the regulations in the park?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is part of their duties, but all infractions of law that are within their jurisdiction come before them.

The police themselves,
I presume, would not be able to provide machinery for that kind of thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend, who is a lawyer, will agree with me, that it is hardly fair to have the body adjudicating that lays the charge.

I was thinking about what happens in New Westminster in connection with another department, Indian Affaire, which comes under the jurisdiction of the minister. I have in mind a difficulty which has arisen there owing to a conflict of jurisdiction between the police magistrate and the Indian agent, and the objection that has been made to the minister by reason of the fact that the Indian agent at New Westminster insists on trying cases for breaches of the Indian Act when there is in the city a police magistrate before whom these cases should be heard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is
out of order in the debate which he is entering on now.

Speaking to the
point of order, I was asking the minister whether it would not be possible for someone in his department or in the department of the police to take care of these prosecutions, and the minister rather laughed at that proposal-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No.
, Mr. McQUARRIE:-and suggested that that would be rather unfair. I am calling attention to something that has actually taken place in another department under the jurisdiction of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is it
rather not the case in which disputes arise, all or practically all the Indian agents have magisterial jurisdiction, are given magisterial jurisdiction? Is it not a fact that most of the litigations that come before them are disputes between the Indians themselves rather than disputes between the agent and the Indian?

What I am speaking
about now-and I prefaced my remarks by stating it-is that the matters that the Indian agent insists on trying are cases of breaches of the Indian Act.
By whom?

Laid by the Indian
agent.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Against
whom?

Against the Indians
or against others who have sold liquor to Indians that kind of cases-all in connection with the administration of the Indian department, the office of the Indian agent there. To make myself perfect-
11 p.m. ly clear, I do not believe in that kind of thing at all. As I have informed the minister by 'Correspondence, I do not believe that kind of thing should be permitted. I think the minister should see to it that the Indian agent does not interfere in that way. It is provided by the provincial statute that where there is a police magistrate, no other justice of the peace or other officer of that kind can hear cases. That is so in regard to the province, and I think the Dominion should do the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Would that not require an amendment to the law?

Not at all. The magistrate is there. The prosecutions may and should be brought before the magistrate.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Does the law say so?

That is what he is
there for and paid for.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext:
The minister states that
the Indian, agent has the jurisdiction of a magistrate to try those cases. Has he or has he not? If he has, he can try them. If there is any reason why exception should be taken to' his jurisdiction, it is up to the man who is brought before him to take that exception. If my hon. friend objects to the Indian agent having the powers of a magistrate, the question would be one of amending the law so as to take those powers away from him.

That is not necessary
at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I rule this debate out
of order. It is on the Indian Act and has nothing whatever to do with this item.

What is the minister doing in connection with historic sites in the Niagara district? Many of the battlefields of the war of 1812, 1813 and 1814 are to-day in the state in which they were nearly a hundred years ago, and while it is true the minister and some of his officials have visited the sites and erected a few tablets, the battlefields are lying there untouched.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not guilty.

When you enter the mouth of the Niagara, you see Fort Mississagua. You would think it was a fort in Belgium after the Germans had passed through. The roof has all fallen in. Compared with the large appropriation which the American people give for this particular object, this is a very small vote for the work the department has undertaken as regards Canada. I urge the minister to take more definite action in this matter. Chippewa was the bloodiest battle of the war of 1812-14. If you go through that village today you will find1 that the battlefield is not marked out. At Lundy's Lane the government erected a small monument. But all these historic spots in the Niagara district should be no longer neglected by the government. I would urge upon the minister that he might well seek the co-operation of the Niagara Victoria Park Commission, which I am sure would do the work for the government at cost prices of preserving and reconstructing these ruins. We might well follow the example of our neighbours, for in the Cumberland valley every legislature is taking steps to erect monuments to mark the battles of the Civil War. The Battlefields
Commission down in Quebec has done excellent work and is a model for Canada and the Empire. Not only this government but the government ahead of it should have done something to mark these historic spots. I would strongly urge the minister not to be stingy in this respect but to go over the Niagara district and spend a few hundred dollars a year to mark the old battlefields and preserve the ruined forts.

The minister said, and quite correctly, that these national parks have no form of local self-government, complete control being vested in the Parks branch at Ottawa. The vast area of our national parks lies contiguous to the Rocky mountains, out of a total of ten thousand square miles less than ten square miles being found in any other part of the Dominion. I think it is important that the largest possible measure of local self-government should be given to the communities settled within the .park areas of Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan. I wonder what the members of this House would think if they were forced to live in a district where the regulations, even those of the most minor character, were all framed in Ottawa? For instance, there is a regulation as to the length of string which you must have on a dog if you are taking it around the town of Banff! The residents and tourists find such regulations very irritating. I think it would be a matter of convenience and result in considerable economy if the government W'ould delegate every possible municipal function to a responsible local administration. By " responsible " I mean an administration elected by the people of the locality. Let these people govern themselves to the furthest possible limit, reserving to the park administration the power of disallowance of any municipal regulations which are found not to be in conformity with the general park policy. Instead of having a few clerks in Ottawa engaged in drafting these regulations, many of them unfamiliar with local conditions, you would then find the residents, who are tremendously interested not only in their own welfare but in the park development, carrying into effect policies wdiich in the long run would make for the best development of our national parks.
I speak of this matter with some knowledge, for I have had occasion to talk with a great many people, tourists included, who happened to come to Banff National park, and I have heard1 some of them express the opinion that certain minor regulations-all drafted in Ottawa-are of such an irritating
Supply-Interior

and irksome character that they do not intend to revisit the park, as when on a holiday 'hey do not want to be bothered with policemen and petty regulations. It is true there is an advisory council at Banff, as mentioned by the minister, but this council is purely advisory. This policy was inaugurated by the preceding administration, and I think this administration might well develop it and give the people those rights of local selfgovernment which they should enjoy as British subjects, and which I have no doubt, would be exercised to the best interests not only of themselves but of the parks in general. I simply make this suggestion because I am hopeful that the minister knowing the local conditions will do something along this line. I am sure it would be a profitable and wise course to take and result in true economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is
rather a vexed problem to solve, for you cannot very well give municipal jurisdiction within the boundaries of a park and still have a park. One of the complaints my hon. friend has lodged has been of long-standing- the regulation against dogs running at large. My hon. friend well knows, because he is at Banff very frequently, that one of the pleasantest sights in the vicinity of the town, sometimes in the streets, is young deer and mountain sheep wandering about, so tame that tourists can go amongst them. If the park is to be made attractive in this way we must have regulations to prevent dogs running at large. There are always two sides to a question, and I have some sympathy with the residents. On the other hand, I have had occasion to look into the matter carefully, and the statement that the regulations are drawn up by clerks in the head office here who know nothing about local conditions is scarcely fair. The regulations are the result of advice coming from the officials who are directly in charge at Banff.
I am not going to deny that an official having unlimited authority may sometimes exceed it, hence some difficulties arise, but I would point out to my hon. friend that it is my desire, as I think it is the desire of the superintendent and the chief officials of the parks administration, that the citizens shall be given the fullest possible privileges, but there undoubtedly must be restrictions. When this matter first came to my attention it was because of two young deer which were wandering amongst the cottages at Banff being chased and killed by dogs. Clearly we cannot permit a recurrence of this trouble.
I have, had complaints from tourists about

the poor dogs being tied up, but if they are to be allowed to run at large we certainly cannot have deer in the vicinity of Banff. I wish to impress upon the committee our desire to meet every reasonable and legitimate request of the citizens of the community. I think in the main we have been doing that. Of course there may be regulations that some people do not like, but we will try to meet the objections as far as we can.

Will the minister let me
know what he is going to do about the Niagara district?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that the Historic Sites Board are working in conjunction with the Park Commission in the Niagara peninsula. It would take a considerable amount of money to repaid such sites as my hon. friend mentions. We are expending annually a fair amount on this work and are gradually accomplishing something in the marking of the more important sites. I am informed that the complaint my hon. friend makes is being attended to as rapidly as finances will permit.

In answer to the suggestion
made by the minister I gave an illustration to indicate the difficulties that arise. The minister suggests that allowing these dogs to run loose results in the deer being chased off the streets. I would remind him that years ago when there were dogs running loose there were also deer going through the streets. The minister has presented one side of the picture, but there are some people in Banff who suggest-I do not know what truth there may be in the statement-that these deer were not killed by dogs at all. It is also suggested that on account of the deer being allowed to run loose to such a great extent the lives of children are often imperilled, and cases are actually cited to illustrate these facts. However, that is not the primary point. The point I want to get at is the question of the distribution of the power so far as municipal affairs are concerned. I think the department would be well advised to give the people in those communities the fullest powers of local self-government that can be given. These people are primarily interested in making their towns attractive to tourists, and if it is desirable to have animals go into the city, why, they are going to do everything possible to have them there. I think that could be very safely done by the government retaining the power of veto, or disallowance, if you want to call it that. This would encourage the local residents to take a greater interest in the affairs of their community and besides it would

Supply-Interior
relieve the department of this long distance method of government. Instead of people having to come to governments-to come say from Banff to Ottawa-governments nowadays should come to the people just a little bit more. Will the minister give me the figures I asked him for with regard to the construction of the lighting plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
Is that above the original
estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is about
the amount of the estimated cost.

Last year when a similar
item was before the committee I asked the minister questions in connection with the Moose Mountain Forest Reserve and the pleasure resort at that place. The minister very graciously replied that the people of southern Saskatchewan deserved a playground and that he was going to do something for them. Well, the whole summer passed, and I am sorry to be obliged to announce that nothing whatever was done at that resort in the Moose mountain country. I see that there is a reduction of $270,000 odd this year and I have wondered if the minister has forgotten altogether about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It does not
come under this item. It has to do with forestry.

The area is divided into
three parts. We have the Indian reservation; back in 1911 we had an area set aside for the purposes of a buffalo park; we have the lakes resort and the timber preserve. The whole are combined on the Moose Mountain Forest Reserve. I am speaking more particularly from the point of view of the pleasure resort. I would like to know in any case what the prospects are this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
Two years ago I asked
questions concerning that, and I think it was stated that approximately $2,000 per year came to the Dominion government from fishing permits, timber permits and various other activities on that reservation. I wish to remind the minister also that we are paying an
annual federal tax of approximately $1,450,000, so I think I am only asking for my right in asking for what we have persistently tried to get since 1909-10. I bring the question up each year, and I may say that my people are not satisfied with the treatment they are receiving at the hands of the Dominion government in this connection. That same forest, preserve is filled with game: We have many moose, elk, jumping deer and various other animals, and when a farmer is unfortunate enough to have his grain left in the stook it is entirely eaten by these animals. I know he would have recourse under the municipal law if it were something his neighbour were responsible for, and I think I am quite right in at least mildly pressing upon the minister the justice of my request.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I was not
objecting to the request; I hope my hon. friend did not take that from my attitude. I was simply pointing out to him that an expenditure of this kind would have to be taken out of the forest moneys. I now have full information before me in respect to the requirements of that locality, and while I cannot perhaps, fully meet his request we propose doing something to assist ourselves, and that will materially assist the people who go in to that particular lake.
How much of this item is for historic sites?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: How much longer does the minister want the committee to discuss this item? I do not like to see him break the rule of his leader, who told us the House would always be closed at eleven o'clock. We sat last night until one. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would like to put this item through and then adjourn.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
